utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, good morning, everyone. Welcome back. I hope -- or we hope suitably re-invigorated to respond to the many challenges, I'm sure, that lie ahead for this year. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, good morning. Happy New Year to everyone. And our first witness this year, Your Honour, will be Adnan Merovci. Your Honour, this witness will testify as a live and a 92 ter witness; 92 ter being his statement, which is Exhibit P2588. There is a supplemental information that we obtained yesterday. He added two new paragraphs or two additions to his statement. I don't know if Your Honours have a copy of that or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We do, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I had indicated in Defence counsel in that that I was going to move to amend the 65 ter summary and seek to lead that evidence live when he testifies today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is there anyone opposed to that evidence being led from this witness? Very well, Mr. Hannis, we will allow you to amend the 65 ter summary accordingly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And we will now hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. One other matter, Your Honour. He indicated to me that he had prepared a one-page handwritten document in Albanian, which is a list of dates with names or events to the side. I made a copy of that and handed it around to the Defence. He indicated to me since he felt some unease certainly on dates that he might refer to it. I indicated to him to let us know if and when he felt the need to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Merovci.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Would you please make the solemn declaration to speak the truth by reading aloud the document which is now before you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated. As I'm sure you know, you're going to be examined, asked questions by a number of counsel here; and in the first instance, these questions will be posed on behalf of the Prosecution. And the first counsel to examine you, therefore, will be Mr. Hannis for the Prosecution. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honour, this witness will be testifying to the paragraphs that are indicated in the notification that was filed last week.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Merovci, good morning. I understand, sir, that you are a Kosovo Albanian, that you are married and a father of four children. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you speak, in addition to your mother tongue of Albanian, you also speak and understand English and Serbian?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry -- yes, thank you. I would first of all like to show you an exhibit that's been marked as P2588. Mr. Merovci, if I can hand you momentarily a hard copy of the English version of this document. Do you recognise what that is?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: Yes, that is the statement I gave and signed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And did you have a chance to review that statement before you came in to court to testify today?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: Yes. I had a chance to read it again, and it's clear to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And are you satisfied it's true and accurate?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: Yes, the entire statement is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And can you attest to the Court today that that is your evidence, and you would give the same answers to those questions if you were asked the same questions again today?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we would tender that statement pursuant to Rule 92 ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Merovci, since the time of your statement, I wanted to ask you about some of your employment. After you left Mr. Rugova, did you have occasion to perform any work for the OSCE?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I was the chief executive of the election secretariat. I was the head of the institution for the organisation of the local election in Kosova.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And those elections were held in what year?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: I'm talking about the election of 2004.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And since that time, have you worked in private industry?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: Before that time, I was a director of Kosova post service. After election, I worked in the private sector where I work even now. I am the executive direct of a foodstuff industry.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, I want to take you to your statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And if I could have the usher bring me back the copy of your statement so I can refer to my notes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In paragraph 1, you make reference to in 1981 you began working for the Bank of Kosovo. What kind of work did you do at the bank?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: I was responsible for the data processing department at the IT sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, you continued to work at the bank until 1990, as I understand from your statement. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: Yes. I worked until 1990, but with one year interruption, during which I served in the military.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That was your compulsory military service with the JNA?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what type of unit with the JNA did you perform your compulsory service?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: I was in the artillery division.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Merovci, I want to jump ahead in your statement to paragraph 8, and you're talking about the 1980s. You say: "Even then it was Mr. Milosevic's strategy to get Kosovars," Kosovar Albanians I take it,"out and move Serbs in so that an ethnically clean province was created." What evidence did you have or what did you see to lead you to the conclusion that that was Mr. Milosevic's strategy?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: Among others, there was a programme, a pre-determined programme, for the return of the Serbs which absolutely discriminated Albanians, and I will provide only a few arguments here. For example, the Serbs could have access to work, they had a place of work, they had accommodation, housing; then there was the law in force, discriminating law, whereby the Serbs were not allowed to sell solid property to the Albanians. These are a few things that come to my mind at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: When you say the Serbs had access to work and had accommodation or housing, how was that different from an Albanian's access to work or housing?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: When I said that they had deliberate discriminating programme against Albanians and favouring Serbs, it was a programme organised by the government at that time, and often it worked against Albanians. For example, if a house or an apartment that was meant to be given to an Albanian working in a certain place - and at the time when I am talking about that was a collective property. There was no private property - such houses or apartments were -- were meant to be given by people working in different enterprises. That happened to me, too. I was -- my name was in a list waiting to get this accommodation, and a colleague of mine came to work and she got a new apartment for a couple of days, an apartment which was dedicated -- which was meant to be given to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And you said that Serbs could not sell property to Albanians. What type of property are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: That is true. There was discriminating law in force which was criticised afterwards even by the international community. In the case of solid property, it was forbidden for the Serbs to sell it; however, there are have been transactions, private transactions made because this law, in fact, was discriminating the Serbs who wanted, in fact, to sell some sort of their solid property. So the effect of this law, in fact, worked against the Serbs, but it also had an effect on the Albanians as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You mentioned that law that prohibited Serbs from selling property to Albanians. Was there a similar law preventing Albanians from selling property to Serbs?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: No. Only the Serbs were prohibited from selling property to the Albanian. So we couldn't get hold of that property through court proceedings, but the opposite could be done.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. I want to move forward to paragraph 11 of your statement, where you talk about in 1989 the formation of the LDK party under Mr. Rugova and others. When and how did you become an activist in the LDK?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: I became an activist of the LDK in its first days of formation. I was one of the first militants engaged simply in technical affairs. My engagement consisted mainly of the organisation of the work of the office for the deceased -- for the late President Rugova. And at no moment did I become involved in political affairs during my entire career in that organisation and in more real terms with Mr. Rugova.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you ever become a member of that party?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: In fact, I was not a member, formally speaking; but given that there was an organisation that resembled more a movement that dealt with the organisation of life in Kosova, the health service, education, cultural activities, and so on, it was a form of organisation which all Albanians ascribed to, because that made possible their life in those conditions.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Although you were not a member, did you eventually come to be paid for the services that you provided to the LDK?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: Initially, every activist worked on a voluntary basis, mainly engaging in activities of his or her own free will. So our activity was based on the personal contributions of each and every one, because at the beginning it was difficult for this organisation to get funds. This went on for the first three years. And in my private car I, drove Mr. Rugova for three years at my own expenses. After that time, we managed to put in place a financing system which was called more, a monthly contribution, and because of that we managed to be paid.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. In paragraph 13 you talk about your employment at the bank of Kosovo and your membership in the Presidency of the trade union. Can you tell us briefly what -- what was the role of the trade union at the bank?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: At that time, a little while before the multi-party system was legalised in Yugoslavia, workers started to organise trade unions. They were called independent trade unions. Each organisation, each institution, even the public institutions, could form such kind of organisation. I was one of the organisers of the independent trade union at the United Bank of Kosova. I was a member of the Presidency of this trade union.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you mention in 1989 the imposition of certain emergency measures, I think sometimes they've been referred to here as special measures, that took place in -- around the time the autonomy of Kosovo was revoked. You're familiar with that event?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: Yes, I am. Following the constitutional amendments, the violent constitutional amendments, all the public, economic, and social institutions, mainly economic, were subjected to violent measures. This is how we described them and this is the word used in Serbian. These measures were imposed on us against the will of the society and the workers employed in these institutions. After these measures, procedures started to eliminate or liquidate --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Correction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- the institutions which might continue for years to declare them bankrupt. The process of assessment went on for years, and then commissions of experts had to decide on the destiny of the enterprise, which implies the liquidation procedure or bankruptcy procedure which, in fact, continued in Kosova in the bank where I worked. I'm talking of the time when Markovic was prime minister and his notorious programme was published.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. You used the term that has been translated into English as violent measures. You said that this was the word used in Serbian. Can you say the word in Serbian so we can hear how that's translated from the Serbian.

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: We called it -- or in Serbian it was called "prisilne mere," coercive measures.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And how did it affect you and other employees at the Bank of Kosovo when these measures were put into effect? How did that work in real life?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: These measures had the objective of destroying all the institutions in Kosova and, especially, they aimed at firing Albanians from work in all institutions. At the bank where I worked, which had about 500 employees, of whom about 300 were Albanians and the remainder Serbs, with the exception of some Albanians who were in key positions in the bank, I was one of them, the number was about 60, we were the ones who were -- who remained in that institution and about 240 others were fired. As I said, I was one who remained in the bank. But after some weeks, I, too, suffered the same fate. I was sacked from work as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Merovci, you have referred a moment ago to the way in which enterprises were bankrupted or liquidated. In the case of the bank, you've described in your statement how the Serbs took control. Once they had control of the bank, why did they liquidate it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Initially, they put in place a programme of violent measures in all institutions. When I say "all institutions," I mean all institutions, including social, state institutions, and others. In the bank then, they started to use the liquidation procedure on the pretext that it was not a profitable bank. I'm talking about the time when this was the only bank operating in Kosova, and it was part of the unity of banks of the former Yugoslavia. And the process of liquidation is applied in an institution only when it is assessed that it is not a profitable institution, which was not the case with that bank being the only one operating there. So by violent measures, I mean the imposition of a violent management.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I don't think you understand my question. My question isn't to understand the process, but to understand the motive for the process. Why, if it was possible to secure control of the bank by dismissing Albanians and ensuring that the Serbs had all the senior positions, why was it then necessary to liquidate the bank, by which I assume its operation ceased?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is my opinion and I base it on fact. I want to explain to you that these violent measures were imposed on every institution and this is a fact. Then, in the case of some institutions, as the case is with the bank being a financial institution, the only way for them to fire employees from this institution, which has nothing to do with politics, was through the process of liquidation. This was the reason why the bank was subjected to this procedure, and all the procedures were conducted by Belgrade. To be clear to all, the liquidation process didn't come about as a result of violation of the state of the bank of this financial institution, but only with the intent of firing the workers from or the staff from their posts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Once the bulk of the Albanian staff were dismissed, did the bank continue to operating under the control of the Serbs? Or did it -- was its business terminated and its doors closed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The bank continued its operation, but not with the status it used to have with a very reduced number of staff. When I say "reduced," I mean taking off all the Albanian staff, and it changed the name as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. I do now understand. Thank you. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Merovci, were any of the Serbs who worked at the bank fired or let go during this process?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: No, not only the bank but in no other institution were the Serbs fired. I don't recall any case of any Serbs being sacked. On the contrary, other Serbs replaced the Albanians who were fired.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I want to move now to paragraph 17 of your statement. This is after you have been expelled from your job at the bank, and you joined Dr. Rugova full time. Did you eventually have a title for the job that you did with Dr. Rugova?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: Yes. I was responsible mainly for the administration of his office, his cabinet. My position was based on the work I did. I was personal secretary of Mr. Rugova. Now and again, I was described as chief of protocol. Sometimes I was described as his technical secretary or personal secretary, but my work consisted of things having to do with the position of a personal secretary.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Was Mr. Rugova your direct supervisor, your direct boss, nobody between you and him?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: My -- I had direct relations with Mr. Rugova. My work consisted only in activities related to his activity.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what kinds of things did you do for Dr. Rugova in that position?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: Since in 1989 Mr. Rugova was elected president of the LDK and in 92 he was elected president of Kosova by the election organised at that time by the Albanians, my work had to do with the organisation of his protocol meetings; sending and receiving documents. I was responsible also for his security. It was kind of improvised security for his transport, and also I had to take care of his family.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In paragraph 19, you mentioned that in the course of travels with Dr. Rugova that you had numerous contacts with the border police or the border personnel. You say: "Sometimes the harassment would be a personal matter and sometimes it would be organised harassment." Can you explain for the Judges the difference between and give us some examples of personal harassment and organised harassment.

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: Yes. In the course of my work, I had to escort him in all his trips; and in all his trips abroad I was with him, I accompanied him all the time. There was a person who had to communicate with the counterparts and to witness harassment or -- by the police. For example, when we went to Macedonia or even when we crossed the border to go to some other foreign countries, this kind of, if I can say, maltreatment or harassment, had a personal character often. When I say a "personal character," I mean that sometimes when they stopped our car - usually, we used three cars; one before, one at the rear, and one with the president in the middle - they allowed, for example, the first or the last car and stopped the middle car, where Mr. Rugova and I was. And after asking us to show our IDs, sometimes it happened that a policeman in secret told me that we did this only because my chief asked us. We don't have an order to stop you, but we just want to prove to you that it is us who are here. And after that, they made comments that we stopped Mr. Rugova, we saw him, and we talked to him, and so on. These were the things that happened to us by the individuals who were charged to do that by the police. When I say that they stopped us and maltreated us in an organised way, I mean that sometimes from Pristina to the border, which is about 60 kilometres, it has happened that they have stopped us seven to eight times on the way and asked us the same questions, communicated to us in the same way, just to delay us. It has happened sometimes that I show them the plane tickets, and when they saw the time of the flight they deterred us even more and we lost the plane. Sometimes we were invited to attend some occasion by international institutions like the European parliament and other institutions. We show them the documents and they didn't show any understanding for our position. When we arrived at the border, we didn't have any problems. So this is an argument that convinces me that everything was staged.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. I want to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It may be that this will be resolved later, but in line 4 I think -- in fact in line 3, the witness said I was the person who had to communicate with the counterpart.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's what I heard too, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Merovci, I want to move to another topic. In paragraph 28 of your statement, you mention that in early 1998, the UCK, the KLA, became more established and more active. Did Dr. Rugova or you ever have any direct contact with the UCK?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: No. To my knowledge, Mr. Rugova had no contact whatsoever with the Kosova Liberation Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, I guess I should limit that, but I understand from other parts of your statement from the Rambouillet and Paris talks that there were representatives of the UCK that were part of the Albanian delegation. But I meant apart from that where you were members of the same delegation, no contact?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: If we are speaking of the time before the war, before the Rambouillet conference, then the answer is no, I did not have personal contacts with them. But these were people that I knew before, before they became active in military ranks.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And Dr. Rugova, likewise, before Rambouillet?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: Mr. Rugova, too, did not have any contact with these people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can I clarify two things just before we move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: In your statement in paragraph 28, you say that one of the leadership of the LDK, Fehmi Agani, did have contacts with the KLA; and you say, according to the English translation, "this was a formal relationship between Agani and the KLA." Now, what do you mean this was a "formal relationship" between them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the late Mr. Agani was one of the deputy chairman of the LDK and a close associate of Mr. Rugova. I would say that Mr. Agani had indirect contacts with the KLA through activists and people who were during one time part of the LDK organisation and then became KLA members. So when I say "formal relation," I refer to this aspect. So these were contacts of a courtesy and informal nature. As for Mr. Rugova, he never had any direct contacts with these people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, I read you as saying not formal, but rather informal contacts with the KLA. There was no established relationship, according to the answer you've just given?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. What you are saying is correct. When the statement was taken, I meant "formalisht" in Albanian, which is "formal" in English. And in a way it changes the character of the sentence, but you are right, Your Honour..

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The other matter is a separate matter in the previous paragraph, which is unrelated to this, paragraph 27. You're talking about the completion of the agreement about education that the communita di San Egidio was involved in. Did Rugova and Milosevic never even meet to sign that agreement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are now speaking of the agreement that was signed in 1996. As you already pointed out, it was mediated by that organisation. It was signed by what is called shadow diplomacy. There was no direct contact between the two, but the agreement was signed first by Mr. Milosevic in Belgrade and then by Mr. Rugova in Pristina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Merovci, sort of going back to a topic we talked about earlier. In paragraph 30 you mentioned that because of the increasing violence in Kosovo, Dr. Rugova had reduced his travel within Kosovo, particularly in the isolated areas, but he continued to travel abroad. And you mentioned that you almost always had harassment on the Kosovo side of the Macedonian border when you came back from these trips and that you noticed that the level of harassment seemed to differ depending on where you had been on the immediately preceding trip. Can you give some examples of that.

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Rugova, with his journeys abroad and his meetings, official meetings I mean - and when I say "official," it means that these meetings were convened; he was invited to take part - in cases of high-level meetings and when these meetings were made public, on return we were treated as VIPs in all other countries except in our own country. We were treated there as enemies, and we were at many occasions harassed due to these meetings. I would like to single out the meeting with President Clinton. Upon entering the border, we were maltreated as never before. Mr. Rugova was taken out of the vehicle several times, three or four times, and then made to enter the vehicle again. Everything was searched, the people inside the car, then the escorting vehicles were also followed. So this kind of maltreatment. If the road was clear up to Pristina, there would be a stop by the police; a stop that had nothing to do with traffic violations, but just to ask questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Could you remind us of the date of the meeting with President Clinton?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't remember the date; but if I'm not mistaken, it's 1994 or 1995. And when President Rugova received the Sakharov prize, it was in 1998.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think Mr. Hannis is anxious that we move on now to 1998 and 1999, hopefully.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I have one question to follow-up on that answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You mentioned the Sakharov prize in 1998. What was that and was there an incident upon your return after that trip?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: You are probably familiar with the character of this prize because it was presented to many other personalities, distinguished personalities. After Mr. Rugova received this prize, as we were coming back to Kosova, we were maltreated by the Serb police at the border. And which -- and this behaviour on the part of the police was an expression of nervousness because Mr. Rugova received this prize. In a way they were trying to say that whatever rewards or prizes you get, they are not valid in this country.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me move on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And are you saying that on the occasion of receiving the prize, he also met President Clinton? Or is the only occasion of meeting Clinton in 1994 or 1995?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The incident after the meeting with Clinton is different. I only wanted to point out these two incidents when we were maltreated.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Merovci, in paragraph 31 you mentioned the Holbrooke-Milosevic Agreement in October of 1998, and that after this agreement was reached Dr. Rugova and you travelled around parts of Kosovo with Ambassador Chris Hill. You mention while on that trip seeing VJ troops in the hills between Shtime and Suva Reka. What kind of troops did you see in that area? Were they infantry?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: Yes. They were mainly infantry troops consisting of different types of tanks, armoured vehicles. They were masked and we could see them every now and then from the road in the mountains where you could only see the barrels of the vehicles; although, according to the agreement, these vehicles had to leave, to withdraw.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In the following paragraph, paragraph 32, you mention that Mr. Milosevic did not stick to the agreement to withdraw troops and you say: "In fact, even more were introduced into Kosovo." How do you know that more troops were introduced into Kosovo? What was your source of information for that?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: My source of information, or rather, the source of information for Mr. Rugova's office was an information centre that was part of the LDK in Kosova. It had an information commission which had an information agency called the Information Centre of Kosova. LDK activists would bring the information from the field to this centre. These -- this information was mainly coming from the area of Podujeva at the border with Serbia, where activists would personally see the movement of the Serb machinery and they would report these things to the information centre. The information centre then would make this information public through the media at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. I want to move next to paragraph 38 of your statement. This is after you have discussed some of the events at Rambouillet, and you discuss how during the three weeks between Rambouillet and the continuation of talks in Paris, you say: "Serbs took the opportunity to amass more troops and equipment in Kosovo, although it was strictly against the Holbrooke Agreement of 1998." First of all, how were you aware of the terms of the agreement between Milosevic and Holbrooke?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: The terms of the Milosevic-Holbrooke Agreement or the agreement itself was crowned with the dislocation of the members of the Kosova Verification Mission, of the OSCE observers. This group or this mission had a task to see to what level is this agreement implemented. The deadline was pronounced. Our activists at the various alteration points followed an enormous number of equipment that entered Kosova from Serbia, and this is a public fact. During that time, over 30.000 troops entered Kosova and the number kept growing. The information came mainly from the activists who were following these developments on the side, counting each and every one of the pieces of equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So again, your source of information is through the LDK's Kosovo Information Centre?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: The main source of our information was the Kosovo Information Centre, but this was -- the information we got was proven by the real facts. After the Rambouillet conference, after the Paris conference, the verification mission made -- the work of this mission made no sense because the Holbrooke Agreement was violated, was breached. So the reality spoke to the opposite of the Holbrooke Agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now I want to move to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is there KVM material on this that you're going to be presenting to us? I don't recollect DZ giving us specific figures, for example, like the figure we've just had.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't recall. I would have to double-check --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: -- his transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can I ask you one other question which is related to this matter, but it's a bit disjointed from the evidence you've been given at the moment. Hashim Thaci is referred to as one of the delegates to Rambouillet. Do you know what position precisely he held in the KLA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Officially, he was the director of the political bureau of the KLA; that is, the KLA had a political division, and Mr. Thaci was the director of this department, or to put it more explicitly, he was the political representative of the KLA.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And how did that position fit in with the other leadership of the KLA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I know from the information we received and from what I read, the KLA had a General Staff and these people were mainly members of the staff, with Mr. Thaci being one of them in his capacity as political representative.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You mentioned the figure of 30.000 troops coming in. When you say "troops," are you referring only to VJ, to the army?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: It is difficult to determine the composition. I mentioned the number 30.000 because even later the assessment of the internationals was that about 50.000 troops were deployed in Kosova. So when I say this, I am not in a position to give you accurate descriptions as to the number of the police and the army, but I think it covers both.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Moving now to paragraph 44 of your statement, this is after the talks in France have concluded and you returned to Pristina, you say that there were huge numbers of Serb paramilitaries everywhere. Can you tell us how you -- your definition of paramilitaries, as distinct from the VJ and the MUP. Who were you talking about?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: The paramilitary groups or paramilitaries in this case mean the people who were carrying legal weapons, or to use a better word, were transparent. The weapons were there for everyone to see. So these people were wearing an undistinct uniform. Some were wearing civilian clothes, some black uniforms, sometimes a camouflage-type of uniform, sometimes the upper part of the uniform was green, the trousers were civilian trousers, civilian trousers. In general, what we recognised as members of the JNA or police whose uniforms we knew or were familiar to us, the rest for us were paramilitaries.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: At the end of that paragraph you say: "In most instances they appeared to have just put on a military jacket or something similar, taken the licence plates off their vehicles, and picked up a gun. Nevertheless, it seemed very organised." Can you tell us how so? In what way did it seem that they were organised or very organised?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: When I say they seemed organised, I mean this, that - I'm talking of Pristina where I was an eye-witness to what happened - in Pristina the units were coordinated. As you might well know, there was an Arkan staff deployed in the Arkan -- in the hotel, in the Grand Hotel. It was a staff that in the evenings organised the activities that they were going to launch. The fact that they were distributed in different neighbourhoods and they demolished stores, restaurants in an organised way goes to show that their activity was organised.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In your answer it's translated that there was an Arkan staff deployed in the hotel, the Grand Hotel. Can you tell us what you mean by "Arkan staff?"

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: Yes. These were things which everybody knew. I personally wasn't in the Grand Hotel myself to see them with my own eyes, but I've heard - and I base this on rumours - that there was a headquarters or a staff there that functioned, because most of the personnel went away. And of the Serbs who remained, some have communicated with some Albanians and conveying information. The Grand Hotel was a forbidden place for Albanians. Indeed, people said that Albanians and dogs are not allowed to enter the Grand Hotel.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In the next paragraph, paragraph 45, you mentioned that the: "Paramilitaries began destroying all Albanian-owned property." How do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: These small enterprises that existed and were property of Albanians, they were destroyed. In the period between Rambouillet and Paris Agreements, I have seen such destruction myself. To give you an example, in Dardania neighbourhood there was a health clinic called Rezonanca that was blown up, and that clinic was in a concrete building. That clinic was completely destroyed because of the explosion put there by the paramilitaries. Other stores, jewellery stores, were broken into, plundered.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Are you aware of any non-Albanian businesses or shops that were destroyed during this time?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: No, I don't recall of any instance of a non-Albanian store being destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And how many buildings or businesses are you talking about? Are we talking about ten or 20 or 100? Can you give us a rough idea?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: For the time we are talking about, the period between -- three-week period between Rambouillet and Paris, these businesses that were destroyed might comprise, let's say, four, five such businesses. I'm talking of Pristina because I didn't travel a lot outside Pristina. But if we talk about the following months or period, then the number might exceed 100 because every one of these businesses belonging to Albanians was destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned seeing these huge numbers of paramilitaries when you returned from Paris. What about the MUP or the VJ, did you see them in Pristina during this time between your return from Paris and the beginning of the NATO bombing, during those few days?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: Yes. The return from Paris is the time when the Rambouillet agreement was signed by the internationals and the Albanians and refused by the Serbs. At this time I saw and met groups of MUP and JNA, Yugoslav army, but these groups were more organised I would say and worked on the basis of a plan. Mainly, these groups were dealing with the ousting of Albanians from their homes, with the paramilitary groups preceding them. Depending on the zone, on the neighbourhood and, as you might say, depending on the composition of the Albanian group that was to be driven out, they employed the tactic of sending them out. If they thought that by you using the police and the army more -- to drive them out more easily, they did that. But in other instances, first, they strike panic among the population with the use of the paramilitaries and the police in the army simply drove them out. This was the case also with us in the neighbourhood where I lived.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In paragraph 46, you mention on the first night of the bombing, on the 24th of March, 1999, that several prominent Albanians were abducted and killed. You mentioned Bajram Kelmendi and his two sons. Where were they from? Where did they live at the time?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: Mr. Kelmendi and his two sons were kidnapped in the night of the air-strikes, if I'm not mistaken, on the 24th of March. And they were kidnapped in their own home in the presence of their family members. They were in the bedroom, actually, when Bajram and his two sons were kidnapped. And the people who did that, according to the descriptions by Mrs. Kelmendi, people of the army, of the Yugoslav army.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And where did Mr. Kelmendi live, what town?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: Mr. Kelmendi lived in the centre of Pristina in a neighbourhood called Vellusha, which is situated in the very heart of Pristina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Your statement, Mr. Merovci, in paragraph 46 attributes these deaths to paramilitaries, but now you're, I think, saying something different, are you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The statement speaks about -- also about cases killed by the paramilitaries. But in the second part of the statement, things are more -- of a more general character. In the case of Bajram Kelmendi, we have tangible evidence. His wife describes who came, how they communicated with the family members, and what uniforms they were wearing. This has to do mainly with Mr. Kelmendi and his two sons. In the case of Mr. Hajrizi and Latif Berisha, who was the chairman of the KLA -- LDK in Mitrovica, that is the leader of branch of peaceful movement, he was killed at home. He was called by some people and his killed on his very doorstep. This was the case with Hajrizi as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And they lived in Kosovska Mitrovica, those two, Mr. Berisha and Mr. Hajrizi?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: Mr. Berisha and Mr. Hajrizi lived in Mitrovica and they were killed there. As I already mentioned, Mr. Berisha was the chairman of the LDK branch in Mitrovica and member of the LDK central leadership; in other words, he was an associate of Mr. Rugova.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In this -- I'm sorry. With connection to these two killings, what was the source of your information?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: In the beginning, the communication was done through phones. The phones worked at that time. This kind of information was distributed through personal communication, but also there were media that had their own reporters who passed us information.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you recall what individuals or what media source you heard about Mr. Berisha and Hajrizi from?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: I don't remember accurately, but during this time we mainly listened to Voice of America, Deutsche Welle section in Albanian language. It was mainly radio because it was easier for us to follow what was happening through radio. The radio or the transistor was the main equipment used by the Albanians in order to inform themselves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think, Mr. Hannis, that the indictment in any event in relation to Mitrovica doesn't make reference to any killings.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's correct. It's only a deportation site.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. But even under the heading deportation there's not a killing; whereas, at least in relation to Pristina itself, there is reference to the kill of people from the 24th of March onwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Correct, Your Honour. I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You mentioned in that paragraph that on the 24th of March, Dr. Rugova's office was bombed. Was it a NATO bomb that hit Dr. Rugova's office?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: On the 25th, a day after the air-strikes, Mr. Rugova's office was blown up, not by NATO air-strikes but by different paramilitary groups. The following day, I personally went there by car and passed by the office. I saw it was demolished and burned to the ground. It was a massive explosion. My personal things and documentation was also burned.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And how do you ascribe it to paramilitaries? What was your source of information about who had done it?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: It is very difficult to state what the source was precisely. This information mainly came by Albanian inhabitants who had gone out to carry out some basic, necessary things for their existence, because it was a period when you could not circulate freely and easily or news -- these were news that were commented later on. Even people who spoke of them could not qualify them properly because the time was chaotic. It was difficult for people to distinguish between different groups.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me move now to paragraph 49 of your statement. In that you say, Mr. Merovci, that all the Serb males were mobilised into some force or another, and this was done in a coordinated manner. What was your source of information about all the Serb men being mobilised?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: The mobilisation in the time we're speaking of was in the final stage, because the mobilisation of Serbs and Serb families started much earlier. This was communicated through the media as well where you could see different groups distributing weapons to Serb families, and this was also clear from conversations we had with Serb colleagues who would mention the weapons they possess. They would carry these weapons in a way that they could be seen. I'm speaking of the times earlier. As for the times during the bombing, I don't think that there was a single Serb who possessed weapon who was not allowed to use it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And are you talking about in Pristina only or did you have information about distribution of weapons outside Pristina?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: I'm talking about Pristina exclusively, because I'm a witness to those events. But from the information I received, similar things happened in the whole territory of Kosova.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Is this information received from the LDK Information Centre that you told us about?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: You know that the LDK had branches in the entire territory of Kosova and held regular meetings between chairman of these branches and Mr. Rugova. These meetings were usually held on Fridays, and the chairman of branches would report on the events in their particular areas. In -- during the relevant time we're speaking of, the activists who were in the field would report, even in writing, about mobilisation and other activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In your earlier answer you said that, at page 28, line 10, that you could see different groups distributing weapons to Serb families. Who was distributing weapons to the Serb families, if you know, what groups?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: It is difficult to tell. These were groups that cannot be particularly designated.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. I want to now move to paragraph 52?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And could we pull up an exhibit, Exhibit 615 at page 31. This is the Kosovo atlas.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Merovci, I'm moving to the 31st of March, 1999. I understand on that day you were at Dr. Rugova's home. On the monitor, I hope in a minute, you'll have a map of Pristina, and I want to ask you about a couple of locations there. Will you let me know when you have it.

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Is that big enough that you can recognise it? I want, first of all, if you can point out --

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: It's okay now.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If you can point out where Dr. Rugova's office was in Pristina at the time. Using that pen, can you just put a number 1 and draw a circle around it for where the office was located hypothesis?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: Dr. Rugova's was here in building number 85 near the stadium. It was exactly here, his office. While his residence, his office --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Correction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- house where he lived, it was in Velania neighbourhood, in this part here.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. You've drawn a half circle on the right edge of the map, and that's where Dr. Rugova lived?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: Based on this map, because I can read here Lagjja e Dodones and Velania 8, I cannot find the exact location but it should be within the semicircle I drew here.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can we take a snap-shot of that and give it the next IC number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be IC114, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Haider.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In paragraph 52 you tell us that on the 31st of March, 1999, the MUP came to Dr. Rugova's home. First of all, can you tell us approximately how many individuals came up and were there when the door was first broken down.

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: Initially, we were with Rugova's family and some friends in the house. We saw that certain organised police and army groups were systematically driving out Albanians from their homes. We knew for sure that our turn will come as well. When these groups came to the first house next to Rugova's house, we all went to a room on the first floor and we could see them demolishing the house of the neighbour and looking for people. When they would find people, they would order them to leave. This is when we realised that shortly they will come to us. When they approached the gate of the house, because the house is encircled and has a metal gate, I took the keys to the gate. I wanted to open the door myself in order to show them that there are people in this house. This is the house of Mr. Rugova but this did not happen, because they broke down the metal gate that led to the garden immediately and they set off in the direction of the door to the house. They wanted to break down the door as well, but I called from inside the house and said to them that there are people in this house. I will open the door, but they gave me no time to do that. They broke down the door as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, we really are repeating what's in the statement rather than answering the question I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me stop you there, Mr. Merovci. Yes, your written statement is in evidence and the Judges have it and will read it if they haven't read it already. I want to ask you specifically: Do you recall approximately how many men were in that first group who came through the door?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: It was a group consisting of approximately seven or eight persons initially, as much as they could go through the gate; and then this number became larger.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you remember what kind of uniforms they were wearing?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: Yes. They were wearing army uniforms, the uniforms of the former Yugoslav army.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What colour and what design?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: These were dark green uniforms, and there were also uniforms of a colour between black and dark blue. They were fully equipped, and they had flamethrowers on their backs.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In addition to the flamethrowers, any other kinds of weapons?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: They had long-barrel weapons, hand-grenades, and short-barrel weapons as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You mentioned earlier that as they were coming through the neighbourhood, you saw them going door to door expelling people; and in your statement further on we know that you were, apart from the trips that you took between the 31st of March and the 4th of May, you and Dr. Rugova were in that house. During that time, did you see any of the people, any of the Albanians, in the neighbourhood who had been expelled, did any of them return during those five weeks?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: No, that did not happen. There was no chance for any Albanian who had been expelled to return to his home.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, you said that that initial group was seven eight, and later on in your statement I think you indicated that there were ten downstairs and ten upstairs. Was that the totally contingent in the house on the 31st of March, approximately 20 men?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: This was a number I was able to see because at that time we were isolated in one room, and we could not see outside the window during the first seven and eight hours who was there outside.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And we have quite a bit of detail about this first day in your statement. In paragraph 52, at the end, you mention a local MUP commander arrived called Jankovic from Suva Reka. In your supplemental information, you tell us he told you something else about who he was and where he was from. Can you tell us what that was?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: Since as in the statement and not to go into details, after waiting for several hours without any communication, without any conditions, without any water, a person of police ranks escorted by two people came. In the area where we were, there were soldiers who were guarding us. This person addressed the group of people who were there, asked them, "Who is the person that represents you?" I replied and he said to me, "You will have no problems. We are here to look after you." And I said to him, "You should be careful. In case anything happens to these people here, you will be held personally responsible." I introduced myself. I said I was Adnan Merovci and asked him who he was, and then he introduced himself and he said he was Major Stankovic from Suhareke. He had police ranks, he was armed. I wanted to make him aware of the situation, but he thought that I was, in a way, threatening him.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you there, Mr. Merovci. I have a question about the transcript. Your answer just was translated as he introduced himself as he said he was Major Stankovic from Suva Reka. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: Yes. He said this, "I am Major Stankovic from Suhareke." The police ranks -- I was not familiar with these ranks, and I could not tell what his rank was without he -- him telling me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I want to clear that up because in your supplemental information we had indicated that you said he identified himself as a mayor from Suva Reka and that his name was Jankovic. Can you tell me now if that was mistaken, the supplemental information is incorrect, and it's not -- he's not the mayor, as a political office, but he's a major in the MUP.

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: No, he definitely was a major from Suhareke municipality. So when I said "Suhareke," I meant Suhareke area.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And was his name Stankovic or Jankovic?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: Now I'm confused and I want to make a correction. His name was Jankovic, not Stankovic. The names resemble one another and that's why I got confused.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, would this be the appropriate time for the break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, it would be, Mr. Hannis. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Merovci, we have to break now briefly at this stage. We will be breaking for 20 minutes. The usher will show you where to wait in the meanwhile, so could you please go with him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And we will resume at 10 minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Merovci, one other matter that was in your supplemental information, there was an additional person in the Rugova house at the time that the -- these police and soldiers came that wasn't mentioned in your original statement. This was a non-Albanian. Can you tell us about Renata Flottau, F-l-o-t-t-a-u. Who was she and how did she happen to be at Dr. Rugova's house on the 31st of March, 1999?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: Yes. Mrs. Flottau is a correspondent of Der Spiegel based in Belgrade. She covers the Balkans. On the 31st, she was at Mr. Rugova's house and interviewed him. During this interview, Mr. Rugova firmly stated that the air-strikes should go on, and it was on the same day that this expedition came and broke down the doors and entered the house. Mrs. Flottau was there. She was there together with the family members. She stayed there until the 5th of April, the day when an improvised conference, news conference, was held on the occasion of the arrival of Ambassador Kotov at the residence of Mr. Rugova to pay him a visit.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And her identification as a German journalist was kept a secret from the men who were keeping you in the house; correct?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: I cannot tell you accurately whether this is so because things evolved very rapidly, and the persons who entered the house didn't identify any of the participants. They just asked us to get together in a hole. This explains why at the beginning they didn't know that there was a German journalist present there, but we, too, didn't feel obliged to declare that because we considered that life and death struggle, at least for the first moments. Later on during this news conference, she joined the other journalists and she went her way.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I want to move now to paragraph 54. You mention a Ljubo Joksic, who you describe as the head of the DB in Pristina, came to the house about 8.30 that evening. How -- did you know him from before?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: I knew him by name because it was a well-known name for us in Kosova, but I didn't know him personally. I met him only once, quite by accident, in a cafeteria, and this very brief meeting -- it was a very brief meeting. He was with a person who I know. This is all I can tell you. So that was the first time for me to understand that that person is Mr. Ljubo Joksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And how did you know that he was the head of the DB in Pristina?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: Because many Albanians were interrogated in what we call informative talks and they passed on the information. The structure was known to the Albanians. I cannot describe to you accurately how his name came to my attention, but Albanians commented on him, on his name, as well as on other Serbs who were engaged in informative talks with Albanians. So the information came to the Kosova Information Centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You tell us that on that night he came with another man who was a man you knew as in charge of the Serbian media centre. Do you remember the name of the other man that came with Mr. Joksic?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: He was a person engaged in the Serbian centre base in the Grand Hotel. If you give me three names, I can tell which is his name, but at this moment I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Were these two men wearing uniforms or civilian clothes?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: Civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, with regard to this group of police and soldiers that were occupying the house and the surrounding area, do you know who was in charge of them on the 31st of March? Was there anybody who introduced himself as the one in charge?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: No. No one introduced himself as the person in charge of this group; but with the arrival of Mr. Joksic, in a way we all understood that he was the top man, the man to communicate with, at least this is how he said also.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. In paragraph 54 you tell us on that night that after Joksic and the Serbian media guy left, that there was "an improvised attack on the house." Why do you say that it was an "improvised attack?" Why do you believe it was not a genuine attack on the house?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: That night when it became dark, we were staying in a room where there were policemen in uniform. When kids wanted to go to the toilet, we had to ask their permission. We couldn't make even a simple move. I'm talking about the beginning and the first night; and then the electricity went out. There was no electricity because there are constant outages. And some shots were heard around the house, and the policemen started to move about the house, going out to the terrace and shooting from there. A whole situation of chaos and noise was created. Kids were scared. There were very young children there. We were all sitting in a room without hearing any explanation as to what was happening. I'm talking about the first night; then at midnight, this person, Mr. Joksic, came again. I -- if I remember correctly, he was alone and he wanted to discuss our trip to Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what trip to Belgrade was that that he wanted to discuss? I think you said in paragraph 54 earlier that he had mentioned that Dr. Rugova should go talk with Milosevic. Is that the trip you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: Yes. In the situation we were, in the true sense of the word, at least in the beginning, we were treated as if we were detainees. We were not allowed to make any move that we wanted. We were encircled by policemen. In such a situation, we felt that we couldn't perform our duties and tasks as leaders, like Mr. Rugova was, and I, as his associate. By this I want to say that the trip to Belgrade came about as a result of a communication conveyed to us to go there and find a solution to the situation created. But the decision to go there was not a decision made by Mr. Rugova. The trip to Belgrade was made, as I said, under the circumstances I described. It was not a trip made under the will, full will, of Mr. Rugova.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes. In paragraph 56 I think you explain that, that Mr. Joksic insisted, in spite of Mr. Rugova's protest. On the 1st of April, then, in paragraph 57, you tell us about the trip in some detail. Let me ask you some specific questions. How big a police escort did you have on this trip to Belgrade? Was it just one car and you and Mr. Rugova and Joksic?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: During the first trip on the 1st of April, in the morning, we were ordered to get ready in a short time and get on the car. There was a car that escorted us behind. We were in the car with Mr. Joksic, and a car that escorted us behind.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what about your families, did they remain behind in the house secured by the police and VJ?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: Yes. Our families remained behind, with the exception of my family and my children, who, on my demand for them to be released and go to Skopje, they were allowed to go and escorted up to my brother's house, where the rest of my family was staying. And they went to Skopje during the time we were going to Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: When had they been released, during the night of the 31st?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: My family was allowed to join the rest of my family, my brother's family, and escorted up to the border on the 1st of April, the day that we travelled. This happened first and then we went to Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You say in your statement that when you got to Belgrade, Dr. Rugova met alone with Mr. Milosevic for about half an hour. After that meeting, did Dr. Rugova tell you what he and Milosevic had discussed?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: First they met for a while and then they invited me to join them. I joined them, and there was a brief communication among us. When we arrived in Pristina, on the same day, we also made some comments, short comments, on that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did Dr. Rugova, sometime that day or later, tell you what had been discussed in his private meeting with Mr. Milosevic [Realtime transcript read in error "Milutinovic"], if you recall?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: When I joined the meeting, the reason why I was invited was that Mr. Rugova wanted to gain time from that meeting and avoid for some time the attention. We had a press release in front of us which Mr. Milosevic insisted on us signing. and Mr. Rugova was hesitating, saying that it is not necessary, then I intervened and said that these are technical issues and that press communiques or releases are not signed. They are just sent to the press as they were. But Mr. Milosevic insisted again, and then Mr. Rugova signed this press release, consisting of two or three lines. And the comments of Mr. Rugova were that this had been going on; that is, a talk and an insistence on the part of Milosevic. But we insisted during the meeting that we be allowed to leave Kosova because Mr. Rugova, as it were, couldn't play his role. He didn't have his associates with him, and that we felt like hostages and that a life struggle was going on. I'm talking about what we felt, our inner feelings at what was happening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: In line 17 there's a reference which is clearly inaccurate. It should be Milosevic and not Milutinovic that's referred to.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I agree. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, when you joined the meeting then, I gather from your statement paragraph 57, it was just the four of you; Dr. Rugova, Mr. Milosevic, Goran Milenovic, and yourself. Was it just the four of you talking?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: Yes, the only four of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I believe you had met Mr. Milosevic one time before this. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: In 1998 there was a meeting initiated by the US embassy in Belgrade. Mr. Surroi Agani and Bakalli were present. I was present, too, but I was dealing with technical issues and I met him in the crossroad.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, on this occasion, when it's just the four of you on the 1st of April, 1999, you spoke to him and told him about houses being burnt and Albanians being attacked and expelled; correct?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: Yes. In such circumstances, I tried to explain to him the situation in Kosova and what the Albanians were going through. I raised the issue of some names of persons that I mentioned, like Mr. Agani, Gashi, Mrs. Tahiri, Mr. Hajrizi, and some other people, for whom it was said that they had disappeared. Nobody knew whereabouts were. I expressed my concern about them and explained to him that the Albanians were being expelled from Kosova en masse. I was talking only of Pristina, about things which I saw myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you tell Mr. Milosevic who was doing this, who was burning the houses and expelling the people?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: During that talk, I raised this issue and wasn't asked who was doing what was happening, but it was implied that it was the work of formal and informal structures. The topic was focused mainly on our demand or on our insistence to be allowed to leave Pristina and Kosova together with our respective families. This was an insistent demand by Mr. Rugova and by myself. And another demand was that we be allowed to have a fixed telephone line which in fact worked until that time, but it was interrupted. These were two requests that we insisted on, and our expression of concern about things that were happening to his collaborators and associates and to the people of Kosova in general.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In your statement, you say you told him that almost 600.000 had left Kosovo. Where did you get that number from? What was your source for that?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: The figures were published in various articles by Information Centre and by the media that I mentioned earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In your statement, you say that Milosevic replied that people were leaving because the NATO bombing, and then you say that you said that this was not the case. Did you tell him why they were leaving, if it was not for the NATO bombing?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: Yes. This was also part of our talk. In light of the situation and the circumstances we were in - and this was not a genuine political meeting. We were not on an equal position. We were driven by -- we were also afraid and furry is a human feeling. We were also concerned about our families - so in this meeting and in other meetings we tried not to irritate, to aggravate the situation further, because this affected our lives and the lives of our families. So in the statement that NATO was the reason for the Albanians leaving Kosova, we had a negative response but a soft negative response. I remember that in a diplomatic manner I tried to explain that maybe it's not very important who is causing this situation, but the important thing is to find a solution. If NATO is the one that is making Albanians leave Kosovo, then why are the Albanians being bombarded when they are going to Macedonia?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Correction: Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And if NATO is causing the bombing, then why are these again being attacked? It was a more of a kind of diplomatic talk, I would say, or exchange of opinions.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. I now want to go to paragraph 60 of your statement. The next day, on the 2nd of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Before you do that --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- Mr. Hannis. Mr. Merovci, it was Milosevic that arranged this meeting. What was it he was after?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I can say so after such a time, even though I was asked several times about this incident -- this event, I think he was after this: He wanted to use Mr. Rugova in a perfidious way, for his ends, and to have the strike stopped. If that failed, then he wanted to kill Mr. Rugova politically. Because attending a meeting organised in such circumstances when he publicly demanded the continuation of the strikes, by attending such a meeting he would go against himself. In a way, if I might say, after so much time has passed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Your reference to what he asked for is this. You say that he told Dr. Rugova that "they needed to make an interim agreement which would allow people to return. Only you and I, no third parties involved." Now, what was wrong with that suggestion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am being asked to make a comment and it's not a question if I understand you right, Your Honour, for me to say yes or no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's not simply comment because Rugova would not respond to that. You say that he -- he stalled for time and didn't accept this proposal. So there must have been something wrong with it and that's what I would like to know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At this meeting, Mr. Milosevic was very severe, used bad words against the internationals. Mr. Rugova kept saying that the international mechanisms are in operation, and it is only you that can interrupt this process. Mr. Rugova proposed that in every communication between him and Milosevic and in the case of an eventual agreement, a third party be present as a guarantor to it saying that I am in a situation that I am now. In a way I am not a relevant factor so my consent may not have an effect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, it's possible to understand why someone being bombed has no good word for the persons bombing him. So let's lay that aside for the moment. What was Milosevic's way out at that stage? What could he have done other than enter into discussions with the likes of Rugova to bring this bombing to an end?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't want to make a comment on your question, but it was the Albanians who were experiencing the tragedy and not him. But given the strict demand of the international community that started the bombing, there was no other possibility, other than accepting the conditions of the international community which had imposed them. We didn't see any way out other than that, and this is what Mr. Rugova told Milosevic directly, that, "You have the key to the solution of this situation."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Remind us, please, what these specific conditions were at that stage, immediately after the collapse of the negotiations in Paris. What exactly were the conditions that he was not accepting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The conditions were well-known internationally. I think there were five initially. I will mention what I remember. You have documents about that. One of those was the return of the expelled people and the creation of the necessary conditions for them; the withdrawal of all Serbian troops, police and army, paramilitaries as well; as well as some other conditions which I don't seem to remember now. But they were public and official conditions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But by that time, was one of the conditions that within three years there would be a referendum on the status of Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. It was a subarticle of the Rambouillet agreement. In fact, the strikes came about as a result of the refusal of the Serbian side to sign that agreement. In one of the subarticles guaranteed by the US Secretary of State Mrs. Albright was that after this agreement in three years' time, a referendum should be held on the future of Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In connection with that, do you recall if one of the five NATO requirements was for Serbia to sign the Rambouillet agreement?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: I can't remember accurately, but you can easily find out. But I know that the pretext for starting the air-strike was the failure to sign the agreement and the fact that they actually started the demands increased, asking, first of all, the withdrawal of all police and military forces. But whether the signing of the agreement was another condition, this I don't remember. But I think it was not, if I remember correctly. Then the agreement was not signed, and as a result of it the air-strike started. And the fact that that happened, that is, the air-strike started, is a logical consequence that things cannot go back to where they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
