utterances.text: In paragraph 58, Mr. Milosevic is reported as saying to Rugova: "Only you and I, no third parties involved;" and then you say: "Dr. Rugova stated they needed to have third parties to ensure the agreement was carried out." Is it fair to say at this point Dr. Rugova didn't trust Mr. Milosevic to honour any agreement?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: The question of this agreement we are talking about was an ad hoc settlement by Mr. Milosevic, with the sole purpose of creating a pretext to have an agreement to demand the stopping of bombing; otherwise, such an agreement was not part of any agenda. It wouldn't be -- have any effect. The fact is that in the condition Mr. Rugova was, he had to have a response. And the response was that this agreement cannot have any juridical or political effect because we are in the situation we are and the international community have put up some demands, which, without failing, the bombing will not stop. Mr. Rugova always insisted on the presence of a third party, but Mr. Milosevic always opposed that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I think you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What I read into all of that, Mr. Merovci, is that the only way out for Milosevic was to capitulate at that stage. They had moved on to air-strikes and, therefore, all he could do is surrender because no one would talk to him.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This was a condition imposed by the international community. The entire thing was done on the burden of the Albanian population, at the expense of the Albanian population. Under this pretext, the Albanian population was expelled in the most brutal way. The Albanians of Kosova were looking forward to the air-strikes, seeing it as the only way out to freedom, and this was the pretext they used in order to expel the Albanians and destroy them and their property.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I think you said in one of your earlier answers that prior to the start of the NATO bombing or right around the start of the NATO bombing, Mr. Rugova had said to the international media that he supported the bombing. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: This is correct, and it can be proven by facts. The interview with Der Spiegel on the 31st is a proof Rugova clearly states during this interview that he wants these air-strikes to continue. On the first day after the return from Paris, it was a Sunday, journalists were waiting for Mr. Rugova at his house, and I remember his words - they were in English - "Now it is time for NATO." And the third argument, the third fact is that when the soldiers entered the house they said to me, "This is the house of the person who wanted NATO."

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What was the gist of the press statement that was signed by Mr. Rugova on this 1st of April, do you recall?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: I don't recall exactly the content, but it is along the lines of peaceful solution to the entire situation. If I'm not mistaken, it only consists of three or four lines. I want to point out again that this is a document addressed to the media. It's not an agreement whatsoever, but it's just a press release, signed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And do you have an opinion that Mr. Milosevic was trying to use this signed press statement by Mr. Rugova to drive a wedge between the different members of NATO as to continue the bombing --

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object to the leading form of the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think there may be substance in that objection, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. Let me rephrase the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you have any idea of how Mr. Milosevic might be trying to use this agreement or this press release that he got Dr. Rugova to sign?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: This press release had no effect. I want to stress again that this statement was signed under pressure. I was invited to join them in the room where they were having this meeting just for Mr. Rugova to gain some time, to prolong this. Mr. Rugova wanted to gain time, and the statement itself was not an expression of his own free will. Under the circumstances that we were in, Mr. Rugova signed it, knowing that it will have no effect. And later on, it showed that in fact the statement did not have any effect whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Shortly after that press statement was issued, did any of the international community members try to get in touch with Dr. Rugova to confirm whether or not he was indeed saying what was in that press statement? Were there inquiries from the internationals?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: The inquiries focused on whether it was true that we went to Belgrade or not, and we confirmed it on the same day because the phone was working. The first thing I did was to call the American ambassador to Macedonia in Skopje, Chris Hill, and I informed him of what happened. So it was confirmed that Mr. Rugova was there. I don't remember that this statement was ever mentioned by relevant structures during that time or later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I think you make a reference to that in paragraph 61 of your statement, which -- it appears you made that phone call the next day, on the 2nd of April, when you got back to Pristina. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: It's on the same day. We went on the 1st of April and returned the same day in the afternoon, and I called Mr. Hill on that same day.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And you say there that -- you described the circumstances you were facing, and Mr. Hill asked you if you were under arrest. And you said you didn't want to say openly but suggested that he should draw his own conclusions. Why didn't you want to speak openly at that time?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: The policemen were at the place where the telephone was, and I knew that the phone was intercepted. And as I already mentioned, we were concerned about our lives. That's why I was careful in my comments and answers. And this is what told him, "They say that they've come here for other purposes; but under circumstances that we are in, you can draw your own conclusions." This is what I told Ambassador Hill and also members of different media.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In that same paragraph you mention Blerim Shala, S-h-a-l-a. Who was Blerim Shala?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: Mr. Shala is an independent intellectual. He's the editor-in-chief of Zedi [phoen] newspaper. He was a member of the Rambouillet delegation, member of the group of independent intellectuals. When he was leaving at the border, the police called Mr. Rugova and asked him, "Do you want Mr. Shala to come back and join you?" And Rugova responded by saying that, "It is his own decision to leave and he can do so," so he left.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, in paragraph 60 you say that on the 2nd of April, Mr. Milenovic - and it's, I guess, Mr. Milosevic's assistant - called you and told you that you should meet with Ratko Markovic. First of all, who is Ratko Markovic? What was his job or position?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: Mr. Goran Milenovic called me and said that we had to meet. Mr. Ratko Markovic was a person who was nobody as a person engaged in the education process. At that time, if I'm not mistaken, he was the deputy prime minister of the Serbian government.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And was he suggesting that you, Adnan Merovci, meet with Markovic or that Dr. Rugova meet with him or both?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: This was a sort of unpleasant communication, because even during this discussion we insisted on being allowed to leave. And our priority was to leave Kosova. They came up with different ideas and subjects. On this concrete case, he wanted to meet us. He said that, "You can meet first and then Mr. Rugova as well." This was a result of the first meeting in Belgrade and the pretext was that these meetings will continue to discuss different subjects. This is at least how I understood it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In paragraph 62 then, a couple days later, on the 4th of April, you tell us that Nikola Sainovic came to the house for the first time and wanted Dr. Rugova to meet with Ratko Markovic. Again, do you know why Mr. Sainovic wanted that meeting to take place?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: This was the first meeting with him, and I mentioned it as a request for meeting. And he insisted that a meeting between Markovic and Mr. Rugova take place. If I'm not mistaken, on the 4th of April, the arrival of Ambassador Kotov to Pristina was discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Ambassador Kotov is the Russian ambassador to Belgrade; correct?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What could or would Ratko Markovic be able to do that Slobodan Milosevic or Nikola Sainovic could not do? Why was it necessary for Dr. Rugova to meet with someone seemingly at a lower level?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: In my opinion, this was in order to gain time and to send the international community a signal that a process is going on, that there is communication going on. But you could tell that these things were not well-organised, that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't want to interrupt Mr. Hannis's examination-in-chief. However, the way he is putting his questions should not be allowed. First of all, he is putting a sign of equal between Milosevic and Sainovic. What is it that Markovic could do and Sainovic couldn't? And how come he now says that Markovic was below Sainovic, when we know that Markovic was the head of the delegation and not Sainovic. This line of questioning is not going to lead us anywhere. This is it and I didn't want to interrupt his questioning. I'm not going to interrupt the answers either, but I just drawing your attention to the fact that this line of questioning should not be allowed because he has included two assertions in his question which is more than enough to make the questions leading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think your point is very easily understood, Mr. Fila, in the context of an exchange that might take place in a civil jurisdiction. But in light of the process that we're following here, these are all matters that can be adequately dealt with in cross-examination. You can point out the inaccuracies at that stage. At the moment, we do not consider this to be leading, and we think it's material which can be resolved in due course as a result of cross-examination. So we will repel your objection but understand clearly the point you're making. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Merovci, you had partly completed your answer. Was there anything else you wanted to say about why they wanted you to meet with Markovic and what it was that he might be able to do that Sainovic and Milosevic couldn't do themselves?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: No. Not then and not even now, I didn't understand him as a person who could do something more. But these were things aimed at sending this signal to the internationals; that the process was going on, that talks were going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Then you tell us there was another meeting on the 5th of April, Mr. Sainovic came; then again, on the 9th of April at paragraph 65, Sainovic and Markovic, Ratko Markovic, came to the house. Did -- was anything discussed, other than stopping the bombing and Dr. Rugova's request to go abroad? Anything else discussed on the 9th of April?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: I want to make a small correction. In the beginning you said 5th of April and now you corrected yourself, 9th of April. This is what happened on the 9th April. But on the 5th April, there was a meeting with Ambassador Kotov and there was a press conference. On the 9th of April, a similar meeting was held along the same lines, and every meeting was opened with our demand to leave Kosova.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And on the 10th of April in paragraph 66, you tell us Joksic had called about locating a couple of Dr. Rugova's aides, and you detail that out. I don't have a question on that. Let me move to paragraph 67. The 13th of April, Mr. Sainovic came again and suggested that Dr. Rugova should meet with Mr. Milutinovic, and you were told that the meeting date was going to be three days later, on the 16th, in Pristina. Did Mr. Sainovic tell you at that time what the purpose of this meeting was to be?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: Yes, this is correct. He informed of a meeting with Milutinovic that was to take place on the 16th in Pristina. I will repeat this again, and I will always repeat it whenever I'm asked. We had become people whose opinions were not asked. We had entered this process in order to be able to survive and live. The meetings and topics that were expected to be discussed were along these lines, what we've already said: To enter an agreement, to improve conditions, to create a body for self-governing, things that had been initiated even in the past through two different groups, G15. On our demand to leave Kosova, it was always said that we could find assistants and bring them here, and this is what happened with two assistants; Mr. Ramaj and Mr. Kurteshi.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. On 16th of April, you got a call from Mr. Joksic from the DB and told the meeting was going to be in Belgrade instead of Pristina. In paragraph 68, you tell us you went there and you met with Milutinovic and Sainovic. And upon your arrival, there were journalists or photographers there. Milutinovic, in your statement, is reported as saying that there was unity among all of us, referring to the government, and complete loyalty to Milosevic; and then he told Dr. Rugova that: "Kosovo is yours." What -- in the context, what did you understand that statement to mean to Dr. Rugova, that "Kosovo is yours?" It seems Dr. Rugova couldn't even leave his house without somebody else's permission. How could Kosovo be his?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: This meeting was as you described. We were told that we have to get ready shortly and travel to Belgrade. During this time, it is true that he said this, and at that time I understood it to be: "You are a person, a leader, of the citizens of Kosova and the responsibility is -- lies with you." And this is how I understood it. He simply told him in a diplomatic way that, Kosovo is yours. But on the other hand, there was our consistent demand to be allowed to leave Kosova, and then we brought up the subject of my leaving Kosova and going to Shkup.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So for the first time there was some movement on that request and they agreed that you, Mr. Merovci, would be allowed to go to Skopje; correct?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: In a way, in such situations, they knew that this would be our first demand, and perhaps they were thinking of finding a solution to make a small step forward. So this idea appeared which did not resemble what we wanted, but at least it softened the entire situation. They thought that I would go to Rugova's assistants and tell them that everything is okay and everything can continue, but that did not resemble the reality.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you say in paragraph 68 at the end of the meeting Sainovic gave you some instructions what to say in Skopje. One was to say that you and Rugova were not under arrest and not to mention Sainovic's name too much. Did he say anything about what would happen to you if you didn't follow those instructions? Or did he simply give you the instructions?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: The issue of my trip to Shkup should explained as follows: In discussing this thing with Rugova, we reached an agreement. And he even insisted that the international community should be informed about the situation we were in so that we would be able to discuss the possibility of evacuating Mr. Rugova and his family. This was the purpose or the reason why we insisted on this trip and supported it. And the purpose of the opponent, of the opposing side, was for us to go there and allegedly inform the assistants that everything is okay and everything can continue normally.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I take it from that answer that you didn't tell Mr. Sainovic and Mr. Milutinovic that you were going to tell the internationals that you and Rugova were under house arrest?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: No. No, I never said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In paragraph 69, we know that you went from the border to Skopje and you were there for a few days. Did you go by yourself? Were you alone on that trip?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: I wasn't alone because I was not allowed to move alone. I was escorted up to the border, up to the border -- in the border point of Kumanova on my way to, and Edmund Kerliu received me there. And I went to his house and on the next day I met the internationals.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So within Kosovo you were escorted, but once you got to the Macedonian border were you alone until you met -- I'm sorry. No one else from Dr. Rugova's house went with you on this trip? That's my question.

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: No. I was escorted by a police car, and at the moment when I crossed the border I was by myself. On the other side of the border, my friend, Edmund Kerliu, waited for me. He was not a collaborator of Mr. Rugova in terms of party collaboration. He was a friend of ours, a citizen of Skopje.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. In paragraph 70, you tell us about in Skopje you met with Ambassador Hill and discussed the situation. He understood and was convinced that you and Rugova were definitely under house arrest. Were you under house arrest?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: At the first meeting I had, I had it with Mr. Ambassador Hill at his residence. The meeting lasted for four hours. We were just the two of us, and the conversation was about the way we went to Belgrade, the circumstances we were forced to go. And we -- while we were describing what happened, we said that we were under house arrest and that I was commanded by Mr. Hill on going to Shkup or Skopje. I met Mr. Hill also on the last day when I returned to Pristina, and we discussed the possibility or talked about the possibility of evacuating Mr. Rugova's family, which was said to be practically impossible, but that was one of the topics of our conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you returned, and I want to go now to paragraph 72, and in a meeting on the 28th of April, 1999, in Pristina at this time. You and Dr. Rugova met with Mr. Milutinovic, Mr. Sainovic, Ratko Markovic, and Zoran Andjelkovic. Did you have any advance notice of this meeting?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: Yes, we did. We were noticed in advance of everything meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what were you told was going to be the purpose of this meeting on the 28th of April?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: The meeting was organised following my return from Shkup after finding out that there were no other associates that could return under these circumstances. Maybe that was their last attempt, to use Mr. Rugova as a -- because of the great pressure brought to bear by the international community to release him. And I can mention here the official calls by the German Foreign Minister, Mr. Fischer, and Mrs. Albright, who publicly called for the release of Mr. Rugova and his family. She said, "I want to see them in Brussels." Under this pressure, I think they wanted to gain something in the sense of talking, organising some structures that would deal with the repairing of his house, the return of Albanians; things which for us seemed very irrelevant, and that we saw ourselves as just useless instruments. And I addressed the participants using the words -- using my statement. And from Mr. Milutinovic, I heard that he cannot answer me immediately about our release, but he promised to give me an answer in 24 hours. And the reply came, if I'm not mistaken, about three days later on the 4th.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me stop you there and ask you a couple specific questions. You say at this meeting Mr. Milutinovic said that he could not understand why people were leaving the city. And you then told him that people were being forced out of their homes, that your own flat had been destroyed, and that the MUP had done it. And Mr. Milutinovic then turned to Sainovic and asked: "Is this true?" What, if anything, did Mr. Sainovic say in response to Mr. Milutinovic's question about whether that was true?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: To argue what I was saying about the events in Pristina, I gave the example of the destruction of my own house, which was free of inhabitants at that moment, because as I said I was at Mr. Rugova's house. So since you are -- you have destroyed my house and I'm staying here, I can tell you that nobody can be -- can feel secure. And the fact is that he asked the question that you cited, but there was no reply, just a nodding of the head and they went on to other subjects.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Nodding of the head by whom and in -- and in which way was it nodding? Was it nodding as a yes or nodding as a no?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: It was a nodding of the head as if to express surprise.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: By Mr. Sainovic?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: Yeah, you might say so.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, I wasn't there. Can you tell us who it was.

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: There were six people there, and the question was asked in their presence. And Mr. Milutinovic asked this question of his own people and they feigned surprise, and then they went on to the discussion of other topics.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You already told us that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Before moving on.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What is the evidence that the MUP had destroyed your flat?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the time when I left my flat, it was the 31st of March. We are talking about the 28th of April. During this time interval, I went to visit my flat twice, escorted by the police,. And the destruction of my flat was seen also by the policemen who escorted me, and they were the witnesses to what had happened. And when I said that my flat was demolished by the army members, I argued this with the fact that during my visit there I met a neighbour of mine who told me in Albanian that this was done by a regular soldier who had with them trained dogs. This is an argument I mentioned, but as I said the people with me saw it with their own eyes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, at line 17 the last part of that sentence is not translated, and I didn't quite hear what he said. "A regular soldier had with them rain."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Trained dogs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, "trained dogs" is the translation. Mr. Merovci, the statement that we have in front of us is that your flat had been destroyed and that the MUP had done it, but do I understand you to be saying it was a member of the VJ who did it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise because I may mix up things sometimes now. In my statement I have declared that it was done by MUP forces, but now I want to correct it because I made a wrong interpretation. My neighbour told me that people in uniform, policemen in uniform, with dogs came here. I don't remember accurately what -- whether she said to me just uniformed people with dogs or people in police uniforms. This is how it really is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You told us that at the end of this meeting Mr. Milutinovic told you they couldn't decide the question about you and Dr. Rugova travelling abroad but needed 24 hours. Other than -- Mr. Milutinovic was president of Serbia and Mr. Sainovic was a deputy prime minister of the federal republic. Who had higher authority than those two to make a decision about you travelling abroad?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: What you said I also said at this meeting. Having a meeting with such senior people, I said, "Why cannot we get an answer, since we are free," as they alleged, "to leave?" And the answer I got was, "You will receive an answer in 24 hours." And my impression was or is that an approval had to be taken about that, but this approval depended on the way our demand was conveyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And was there some sort of document signed by Dr. Rugova and Mr. Milutinovic at the conclusion of this meeting on the 28th of April?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: We are talking about the document which has been presented before when Mr. Rugova, late Rugova, mentioned that there was a press release. To be very sincere, that document was signed not in my presence. I was in the corridor dealing with the journalists who were waiting for the delegation to come out. The document was meanwhile signed; and to be very frank, I learned of it during the testimony of Mr. Rugova in this chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And have you seen that document since time that, since April of 1999?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: If I am not mistaken, that document was presented during his testimony, because at the time everything was followed through the media and this is where I saw it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could we show the witness Exhibit P416, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: While we're waiting for that, in your statement you said about 30 hours after this meeting you got a call back saying that someone told you that they were going to meet with Slobodan Milosevic to resolve the issue, your travel abroad. Who called you back?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: First, Ljubo Joksic was the one. He told me, "Your request has been approved and that you will be allowed to leave;" then, if I am not wrong, it was Mr. Sainovic who also called me and informed me of the same thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now we have the exhibit, 416, on the screen. Do you recognise that document?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: I saw this document on the screen, as I'm doing now, during the testimony of Mr. Rugova. And if I am not mistaken, this was also in the form of a communique, and this is how it was called, "Joint Statement," as it is here, and it was read out to the journalists. But I want to repeat that I didn't witness the actual act of signing it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you have any doubt that that's Dr. Rugova's signature on that document?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: From what I see, no. It is his signature, but as I already stated, at the time it was signed I was outside in the corridor, because you know it takes a couple of seconds to sign a document. I didn't say it for any other reason than to say that I was not there when it was signed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Did I note you correctly as saying that this was the same joint statement as had been signed with Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. The joint statement is a title of the statement, that was a Serbian word which means joint statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I recall the answer I think Your Honour is referring to and I had the same thought in my mind, but I think it's clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The statement that was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Merovci, you -- the question was: "And was there some sort of document signed by Dr. Rugova and Mr. Milutinovic at the conclusion of the meeting on the 28th of April?" And your answer was: "We are talking the document which has been presented when Mr. Rugova mentioned that there was a press release." So it's a different -- it's a different press release from the one that you're talking about at the -- following the meeting with Milosevic. Is that correct? The Milosevic one was plainly much shorter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's correct. There are two different statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. We had also listed, Your Honour, Exhibit P833. I wanted to show a connection with this. It's a media report of this meeting and who was present. I don't intend to show it to the witness. I just wanted to indicate that I'm offering it to corroborate his report of who was at the meeting?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In paragraph 73, Mr. Merovci, you say that Joksic called saying that you should be ready to travel to Belgrade again, and that you and Dr. Rugova went and met with Mr. Sainovic. What was the purpose of this meeting on the 4th of May?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: As we were told, that was supposed to be a meeting which would finalise the details of our trip. We insisted that we move together as a family, but were told that, first, it was our turn to go and agree on that issue. We agreed and we went on the 4th of May, but we noted a tendency to separate our families from us, that is, Mr. Rugova and myself, something which we categorically refused. We didn't want to leave them because we wanted to leave Kosova as families. And Mr. Milosevic supported this, and I think that his decision was to allow us to leave together as families, Mr. Rugova and myself. And we flew to Rome on the 5th of May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I thought you said earlier that your family had gone on the 1st of April to Skopje.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I say "families," I am talking of Mr. Rugova's personal family, close family, and some relatives of his. I'm talking of a group of some 16 people; that was the composition of the group. If you give me some time, I may give you their names, but I know it was over ten members.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, paragraph -- so you then were allowed to leave and all went to Rome on the 5th of May, you say? The day after you arrived in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In paragraph 74 of your statement, you tell us that you had conversations with Mr. Sainovic throughout your period of confinement. And in one of those conversations, you told Mr. Sainovic that he might end up in The Hague as a war criminal. Was there any response to that when you told him that?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: At those meetings, which often were informal meetings, I might say meeting sometimes among humans because we all were humans, we discussed about many things. We discussed also Recak and his name and I mentioned that, and he responded again by saying that this was played by Ambassador Walker.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: In that connection, you say that Mr. Sainovic claimed that the KVM had existed exclusively of military people who had installed locators to assist NATO. Is that a -- perhaps a mistranslation. "Had existed exclusively," did you mean to say "consisted exclusively"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is not my statement. I may say that this is speculation by a Serbian circle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, but you're quoting what Sainovic said. So what was it he said about the military people? Could you tell me again to clarify it, because the English in the statement's not clear.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I said, these were talks of an informal character, brief talks when we were entering or leaving the rooms. And one of those was about the massacre in Recak, and the response was the one I mentioned. But it was also said that the mission had in its composition -- had done also this, that is, located places which were later bombed by NATO. This was said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Merovci, in paragraph 76 of your statement, you mention MUP tactics of propaganda that prominent people had been killed, and you say this was done to scare Albanians. How did you know about this? What was your source of information?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: That was a campaign to strike fear. Symbolically putting it, I may say that every Albanian - I'm talking of citizens living in their homes and cities - had to save their lives and the lives of their relatives. Such a campaign proclaimed also through some primitive ways to strike fear among the population to make cleansing easier. I may illustrate this by a pamphlet that was distributed during the first days of the air-strikes alleging that KLA and Mr. Rugova had issued an instruction to the population, saying them -- saying to them to leave Kosova. But this pamphlet was rejected even earlier because there are two things which are incompatible. The KLA and Mr. Rugova had opposite stance, politically speaking, and this pamphlet had errors in it, such errors that make it clear that it was not prepared by the people who had allegedly issued a that call.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I will stop you there and if we can show you Exhibit P839. To follow-up on that, I will ask you some questions. You have seen this pamphlet; correct?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I have seen it, because they had distributed it in various places, in streets, in doors, thresholds of various houses. So if it was a pamphlet that was written by Rugova, I would be the first to know it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I see we have a handwritten version. Can we go to another page of the exhibit. I think we have an English and we also have the original?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did Dr. Rugova have anything to do with this pamphlet that was on UCK or KLA letterhead and apparently called on Albanians to evacuate Kosovo and go to Macedonia and Albania?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: No. This is far from the truth. This has been refuted also by the KLA and by Mr. Rugova. If we talk about the first letter, this is handwritten in Cyrillic letters, and it's -- doesn't stand to logic that you write some -- a letter to the citizens in Cyrillic letters. It's a very primitive way of doing it. As to the other, as I said, it's a pamphlet put in a better shape because it has the original letterhead of the KLA and an improvised text, which in Albanian had many grammatical errors.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I think there may be one more page that shows the original in Albanian. Is that available on e-court? I see we have now the handwritten Cyrillic version in the English version, but I think there is another printed version in Albanian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, we'll break here I think, Mr. Hannis, and the reason for that is there's little point in telling us that there are many grammatical errors in the Albanian unless they're pointed out with a view to some assessment being made, if you think that is of importance.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No. I want to put it on the screen and that's all I have on my direct examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well. Put it up on the screen before we go.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: It's up now, I believe. It's not a very good copy, but there it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Before we go, there is just one question I would like to ask you, Mr. Merovci, and that is: On the 4th of May, did you meet Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. It was a very brief meeting, just to inform us of the planning arrangements -- of the trip planning arrangement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And Rugova was with you at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In fact, I was with Mr. Rugova.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. And was there any stage on the 4th of May when Milosevic and Rugova were together and you were not there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't remember because this was simply a technical meeting just to inform us of the travel arrangements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, we'll have to break again at this stage for half an hour, so could you again go with the usher and we'll resume at 5 minutes to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness be asked to state again the beginning of the sentence because the interpreters didn't get it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Merovci, the interpreters missed the beginning of that. Could you repeat what you were saying, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a request for you, and this has to do with the time of my testimony. I came here on Saturday, and it was very difficult for me to find this time to testify here. I would kindly ask you, within the time-frame of your work, to be able to conclude today because I have a lot of professional commitments to take care of. So I would like to ask you for your understanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We'll consider what you said in our break, but it's very unlikely that it will be possible to oblige you. It's likely your evidence will be concluded tomorrow, but not today. However, we will look at the position and explain it further to you when you come back. Meanwhile, could you leave with the usher and we'll see you in half an hour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Before the witness comes back, Mr. Hannis, can I take it that you were unaware of the request that was made a moment ago?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I am. I was. Can you tell me now what the request is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, sorry, the request that the witness made that his evidence be completed today.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I had spoken with him yesterday, Your Honour, and told him we would do our best, but I thought it was likely we would go into tomorrow. Your Honour, while I was on the record, I wanted to introduce a couple of people. Michael Hehn, on my far right, is from our LRT and research team. He's an intelligence analyst, and I asked him to sit in today. And to my right is Priya Gopalan. She is an associate, a legal officer, with our team.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hannis. Let's have the witness back, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Merovci, your request to complete your evidence today came as a surprise to us because there will be cross-examination. There are six accused in this case, and each has -- is represented by counsel. They won't be examining you -- each one won't be examining you for the same length of time as the Prosecution, but we have to strike a fair balance. So inevitably the time that cross-examination will take in this case will lead us into tomorrow. What I can say is that we will make exceptional efforts to complete your evidence tomorrow. Should it appear that that's not going to happen in the ordinary course of a sitting, then we would accommodate your request and make sure that we finish tomorrow. But there's absolutely no question, I'm afraid, and I'm sorry about this, but absolutely no question of being able to complete your evidence today. So please bear with us, understand the situation, and help us to make as much progress as we can as quickly as we can. One of the things you will find is that if you concentrate on the particular question you're being asked and answer -- confine your answer to the question that counsel's asking you, you might find that we get through the evidence a bit more quickly than we have done so far. So we are grateful to you for your indulgence and thank you for that. Now, Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, thank you. We'll follow the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. Good afternoon, Mr. Merovci.

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Sir, in your testimony, you said you had been an employee of the United Bank of Kosovo. And my question is: Do you know the name of that bank in the Serbian language? What the name of the bank is in Serbian, could you tell us?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: Yes. It was called Udruzena Kosovska Banka.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know whether that bank was in the Belgrade banking system, the Beogradska banking system or the Yugoslav bank system? Do you know which one?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: For the relevant time, two bank systems existed; the commercial or state banks and the United Bank of former Yugoslavia, which comprised all the united banks of the six republics and two provinces. There was also the People's Bank of Yugoslavia that had six plus two popular banks, which dealt with legislative matters of the bank system.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Thank you for that. Sir, in your -- in your statement --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, the question hasn't been answered, though. That doesn't tell us which system this particular bank belonged to, if that's important to you, of course.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This was the United Bank of Kosova. It was a state or commercial bank, which dealt with the development of economy in Kosova. There were other branches of other banks, like Jugobanka, Investbanka, and Beogradska Banka which were a totally different kinds of banks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That helpfully explains that it was part of the first category that you mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Sir, in your statement, the one that Prosecutor referred to, the one that you looked at before coming in, in that statement at paragraph 64 - and you don't have to look at it - you say that you saw meetings on television where you saw Mr. Milosevic and other people like Mr. Milutinovic, Momir Bulatovic, Mirko Mujanovic, and others. Do you recall seeing that on television in 1999?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: This is about a body that was communicated to the public, like a crisis headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And you saw this on RTS, Radio Television Serbia. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: I don't recall accurately on which television, but until the bombing started there was the Kosova Radio Television, which was under the control of the Serbian authorities and under these oppressive measures. As I said, I don't recall accurately on which television I saw this, but it is possible that I saw it also on the Kosova Radio Television.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: So you think you may have seen it either on RTS or the local Kosova television. Is that correct, just to be clear?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: The local Kosova television, as you call it, was a TV station controlled by the Serbs during the relevant time. And in my understanding, everything was controlled by the regime.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And I want to ask you about what you saw on the television. You would see -- is it correct that you saw Mr. Milosevic sitting at the head of a table, and to his left and to his right was this group of individuals sitting at a long boardroom table. Would that be a fair description of your recollection of what you saw on television?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: This was a very short fragment of -- or clip, only a couple of seconds long. I cannot describe accurately how those present were sitting, but I know that that was chaired by Milosevic. And the persons who attended it, I know them --

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: All right --

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: -- and I've mentioned them in my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And I believe you saw this on television more than once. You didn't only see one clip. You would see it from time to time on the evening news. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: No. I saw this only once. These fragments and communiques from this body were not very frequent; and for the time-frame we're speaking of, the television was closed down and we were unable to follow the news.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Now, Momir Bulatovic who you saw, he was the prime minister of the federal government; correct?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: Momir Bulatovic came from Montenegro, but I do not recall the function he performed.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: During this television broadcast, do you recall seeing Zividan Jovanovic at the table? He was the Foreign Minister of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: You're saying "in these," and I'm speaking of a clip that I only saw once. And what I can state here is only what I've already stated in my statement. It is only a couple of seconds long clip.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: I'd like to move on to the meeting held in Belgrade with Mr. Milosevic on the 1st of April. All right. Now, looking at your statement, just to set the context, you joined the meeting with Mr. Milosevic and Mr. -- Dr. Rugova about 30 minutes after it started. And you remained in that meeting for about one hour with Mr. Milosevic, Dr. Rugova, you, and Mr. Milenovic, Mr. Milosevic's chef de cabinet; correct?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: When you say "one hour," it is generalised. It is in approximate terms under those circumstances. It is probable, though, that it is the case. It is true that I joined the meeting upon request by Mr. Rugova. I attended this meeting for not more than 15 minutes maximum. In general, if you take the meeting in general, you can say that it was about one hour long.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And this is a small point, but just the name of Mr. Milosevic's chef de cabinet -- your statement says Milenovic, but it's correct that his name is Milinovic. Would you accept that, one letter different?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: I accept that. Yes, it's correct. Goran Milinovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Now, you said that during this meeting when you were there, after you had joined it, Mr. Milosevic said he wanted to make an interim agreement with Dr. Rugova which would allow people to return. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: When I joined the meeting, the word "agreement" was not mentioned at all. Mr. Rugova just showed me a piece of paper titled "press statement," and he said that they want him to sign this press statement. And as I mentioned earlier, he wanted to gain in time --

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: I'll stop you there. I'm not interrupting you to be rude, but, sir, at paragraph 58 of your statement is -- I'm quoting it back to you to set the context for further questions. At paragraph 58, you've adopted this statement as being true and accurate, and it says in paragraph 58: "Milosevic went on to say to Dr. Rugova that he and Dr. Rugova needed to make an interim agreement which would allow people to return." I'm just asking you to adopt that as true and accurate; that's what you said?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: This is fully correct. But when you say that an agreement had to be made, it does not mean that this press statement was the agreement. This is the point I wanted to make.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: I don't believe I asked you that question, and I haven't even mentioned the press statement, sir. Now, again in paragraph 58, you say that Dr. Rugova said he needed to have third parties to ensure that the agreement was carried out, he needed to consult his colleagues, and that he had no contact with his colleagues and his aides at that time. Now, that's correct also, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: You can say it's correct, but you cannot answer it by yes or no. If you are putting it to me that there was an agreement, my answer is no, categorically no. This was the first meeting. During this meeting, a press statement was signed; and also during this meeting, a possible agreement was discussed. And Mr. Rugova emphasised that there cannot be any agreement without the presence of a third party.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And some of Dr. Rugova's colleagues, his aides with whom he did not have contact, were -- some were in Kosovo and some were in Macedonia, correct, at that time?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: More than 90 percent were not in Kosova from his close associates.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Sir, I wonder if you could focus on my question, and it will go much faster and much smoother. I was just suggesting to you that some of his colleagues were in Kosovo and some were in Macedonia. I think you can answer that yes or no.

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: When you say "some were in Kosovo and some were in Macedonia," I cannot answer that by yes, because you should define the word "some." How many do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Well, are you -- can we agree, regardless of the numbers, that some were still in Kosovo and some had gone to Macedonia?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: I would agree with the following: That the majority had left and only a few had remained in Kosova.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: At one point in that meeting - again, I'm quoting your words from paragraph 58 - you told Mr. Milosevic that Mr. Rugova and you needed to go abroad to make contact with key people and to work on peacefully resolving the situation; correct?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: Our request had to do with our leaving, and we had to justify the request for leaving.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Now, you have mentioned the statement, and you say in your statement to the Prosecution, the statement that Mr. Rugova and Mr. Milosevic signed. You said that: "Before he signed it, Mr. Rugova read it over and he found it acceptable and then he signed it." Correct?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: Mr. Rugova was under pressure. As I already said, he called for me, for me to attend this meeting as well. You know, I was only technical staff there; but as Milosevic was insisting on him, he was forced to formally, officially sign this statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Can we put Exhibit 1D59 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And, sir, you said that the statement signed by Mr. Rugova and Mr. Milosevic was rather short, and I'm suggesting to you that the text of that statement we'll see in a moment, 1D59. I'm sorry. I don't have this text in your language. It's only in English and in Serbian, so I hope you can perhaps follow the Serbian at least. I don't have the Albanian, I'm sorry. Right now I don't have anything.

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: The original was in Serbian as well. I don't mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Well, on the left of the screen, sir, that's the front page of Politika, the Belgrade daily newspaper?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Can we go -- show the right side, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: You can see that it's the 2nd of April, 1999. You see Mr. Milosevic and Dr. Rugova sitting together.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Now, can we focus in -- can we enlarge the picture of these two gentleman and the text above it with the signatures to help everyone see it. Can we go down so we can see the text -- up, sorry, up, up. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And there it says: "President of Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, Slobodan Milosevic, has received Dr. Ibrahim Rugova in Belgrade in discussions about of problems in Kosovo and Metohija. It has been fully agreed that they are both committed to the political process and that the problems can be successfully and permanently resolved only through political means." So that's the short text that you had described earlier this morning, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Now, I think you said many times that starting with this meeting with Mr. Milosevic there were two issues or two concerns that Dr. Rugova and you had. The first was leaving to go abroad and the second was locating Dr. Rugova's aides and colleagues. Would that be a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And during this meeting with Mr. Milosevic, you gave him a list of some of the aides that Dr. Rugova was anxious to communicate with; correct?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: I didn't give him a list but I mentioned names orally, and he wrote those names down on a package of cigarettes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And Mr. Milosevic told you that he would have his security people try to locate those people for you; correct?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: Yes. This is what he said. The first name we asked for to be located was Fehmi Agani, who was later killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And on 10th of April, you were informed by Mr. Joksic from state security that two of Mr. -- or Dr. Rugova's aides, Abdyl Ramaj and Ilijas Kurteshi, had been located. You went to see them in. You brought them to Dr. Rugova's house; correct? That's paragraph 66 of your statement.

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And you also told us that the journalist Mr. Shala, Blerim Shala, a man who shared a moderate view of politics, the same type of political stand as Dr. Rugova, had been located. And Dr. Rugova said it's up to Mr. Shala whether he comes back to Pristina or not; correct?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Now, you've told us that you actually went to -- abroad on the 5th of May when you flew from Belgrade to Rome. But as early as the 5th of April, when you met with Mr. Sainovic to discuss going abroad and locating Dr. Rugova's aides, you were told you were free to go abroad but your security abroad remained an issue. That's what you were told on the 5th of May -- 5th of April, excuse me, paragraph 64. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's not a precise --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just a moment --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have mixed up the dates.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. My objection is that it's not a precise quote. It's that your security -- "We cannot guarantee your security, not necessarily your security abroad. It may mean your security in Kosovo or Serbia as well."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, perhaps precision in the question will get the answer clarified from the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: On the 5th of April, you were told by Mr. Sainovic, "You're free to go but we cannot guarantee your security." You were told that on the 5th of April; correct?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: You mixed up the dates. You said 5th April and then 5th May. On the 5th April, Ambassador Kotov was there and we had a meeting. Later on, the issues that you mentioned were discussed, including the issue of my security, that it can be endangered during this trip.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Right. But in fact on this -- between the 17th and 21st of April, you did travel to Macedonia, where your family was located, where you had contact with some LDK people and some international diplomats; correct?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. I went to the house where my family was staying, in the house of Mr. Nushi Kerliu, who I mentioned earlier. There I met with only two LDK activists. The entire visit or meetings that I had with Rugova's aides were confined to these two activists. The other meetings were with foreign diplomats and journalists.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: I'd like to talk about the late Dr. Rugova for a moment. In your statement, you describe him in these terms, paragraph 11: "He was a very stable, democratic, non-radical politician. I saw Dr. Rugova as the person who would be able to lead the Kosovars and deal with matters democratically and peacefully." Now, this is what you said about him in 1989, and I assume that was one of the reasons you were attracted to him and worked with him. Is that fair to say?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And would it also be fair to say that as a politician, Dr. Rugova's guiding principles were political dialogue and taking concrete action through peaceful means?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: Fair, that's fair.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And would you also say that it's fair to say that Dr. Rugova's approach to politics remained unchanged throughout his life until his death last year?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: I departed from him at the beginning of 2000; therefore, I can talk about that and comment about him for that time. After 2000, the legal internationally recognised institutions were organised in Kosova and Mr. Rugova had posts that I was not involved with, but I am in favour of what you put to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And would it be accurate to say that Dr. Rugova was a key spokesman and interlocutor for finding solutions on issues concerning Kosovo, and one example out of many would be the work he did with Monsignor Palija at St. Edigio on education matters?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: Up to that time, yes, you can say that. But with the appearance of the KLA on the scene and its activities, things changed, because it was seen that Mr. Rugova's policy was such that they didn't -- it didn't go with them, didn't agree with KLA. Therefore, its influence waned. But as to the agreement you mentioned, it was an expression of the good-well of Mr. Rugova as an argument for his peaceful politics because that agreement had to do with the freeing of facilities that were occupied, I mean education facilities, that were occupied by the regime. That agreement was never implemented fully.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Would it also be fair to say that the institutions that Dr. Rugova tried to establish were for all nationalities and groups living in Kosovo? Would that be a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: Yes, it would because we held referendum and elections. And if you allow me to recall that as a result of these elections, we had a parliament and there were seats reserved for the Serbs and other nationalities, even though they didn't participate in this election and the election was not internationally recognised.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Another important approach to Dr. Rugova's politics was to establish mutual trust among communities in Kosovo and with the authorities in Belgrade; correct?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: At first, Rugova was "a monster for the regime," but later maybe they changed opinion, and so that he was a man with authority who followed an approach that was acceptable to the entire world.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: We've seen from your statement - and you've mentioned it here - that Dr. Rugova met with Russian Ambassador Kotov in early April. And while you were away in Macedonia, you know that he met with Patriarch Aleksey of the Russian Orthodox church; correct?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: I have to ask you something that is intriguing to me about Dr. Rugova, and that was his tradition -- the tradition he had of presenting a gift, a crystal, a rock containing precious minerals when he met certain individuals. Why did he do that and what did it represent for him?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: It was his passion, then it became a symbolic gesture for him. Any time he met someone, he made a gift of such a rock as symbolic representation of Kosova's riches because, for your information, Kosova is very rich in such minerals.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: In the spring of 1999 when the war broke out, would it be fair to say that Dr. Rugova believed that it was important to restore peace?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: Can you repeat the question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Well, once you found -- once Dr. Rugova found himself, all of you, in a war in the spring of 1999, Dr. Rugova believed, did he not, that it was important to restore peace?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: This was the case until the Paris agreement. With a failure to sign that agreement, it was the end of the process. And with the beginning of the air-strikes, in a way, a solution was imposed. But Mr. Rugova's definition was always in favour of a peaceful way.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Do you recall, sir, that at the beginning of April 1999 - focus on the beginning of April 1999 - in the period between western and Orthodox Easter, which at that year fell at the beginning of 1999, there was a unilateral cease-fire declared by the Serb side, do you recall that, in the media?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: No, I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Well, maybe I can refresh your memory?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Can we have 1D36 on the screen, please. 1D36. I see the Serbian version on the left and the English will come up in a moment I hope.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Sir, what you're looking at is a joint statement of the federal government and the government of Republic of Serbia, and I can represent to you that the date on that document is the 6th of April, 1999. Now, in the middle of the page, paragraph 1, is the reference I made a moment ago to the unilateral cease-fire that both the federal and the republic government had adopted. And if you go up the page and look, you can see that the second paragraph refers to the meeting between Mr. Rugova and Mr. Milosevic on the 1st of April. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And then the next paragraph refers to the meeting between Mr. Rugova and Mr. Sainovic on the 5th of April, a meeting we've already talked about. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And if we go down to the bottom of the page, you'll see paragraph 2 is there. And paragraph 2 makes reference to, states that: "The government represented that it should immediately embark upon preparations for a political agreement in cooperation with representatives of those Albanians represented by Dr. Ibrahim Rugova, as stated under A, wishing first of all to achieve a simple interim agreement enabling the functioning of joint self-governing authorities in Kosovo and Metohija with Albanian and Serbian national community and the other national communities. That agreement would, after a certain period of time, be a basis for lasting, substantial autonomy in Kosovo and Metohija within Serbia." Paragraph 3, which I won't read, makes reference to the return of refugees. Does -- is your -- are you familiar with or do you recall this declaration and the declaration concerning the simple interim agreement?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: This is a first time for me to see this document; but as I see it, it doesn't seem to be the agreement. It's something -- a document issued by the two senior leaders. But as the document, as I said, it is the first time for me to look at it, and I don't have any comments because it seems to be staged and doesn't contain the approval or the statements by Mr. Rugova, at least in this text I see here.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Very well. I'll move on. Now, you mentioned in the questions by Mr. Hannis earlier this morning that on the 2nd of April, when you returned to Pristina in Mr. Rugova's home and the phone was we stored, Mr. Milinovic, Mr. Milosevic's chef de cabinet, phoned you and asked you to meet with Dr. Ratko Markovic. Now, you know that Dr. Markovic was the head of the Serb FRY delegation at Rambouillet; correct? You have no answer. You knew that, you knew that Professor Markovic was the head of the delegation at Rambouillet?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: Being the head of delegation in this case was a question of something that the Serbs had to decide, because there were no direct meetings between Serbs and Albanians. This was something that they decided. We heard that he was chief of delegation, but it was never officially made it known to us, just as Mr. Thaci was the head of the Albanian delegation.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Right. You knew also that Professor Markovic was one of the deputy prime ministers of the government of the Republic of Serbia? You knew that?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: This name has stuck to my memory mostly because of the talks on the question of education, but what you are saying afterwards, are things I cannot tell you. I cannot deny it but I don't know what posts he had.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Are you aware that he was an eminent scholar and Professor of constitutional law?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: No. It is the first time for me to hear that.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Do you know that Professor Markovic was the head of delegation established by the Government of Serbia established in 1998 to attempt to negotiate a political settlement with Kosovar Albanian leaders?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: If we are talking about these talks which have been held and are publicly known, he was there, but I don't recall that he was a leader. By this, I want to say that the importance of these talks came to nothing because they didn't have any effect at all. To tell you the truth, I don't remember accurately. As I said, I'm not denying it. I know that he was one of the people that led these talks, but I cannot say whether he was the head of the delegation.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Well, you must have known if you were working closely with Dr. Rugova that in 1998 Professor Markovic, as head of this delegation, had written to Dr. Rugova and other Kosovar Albanian leaders to attend meetings with the Serb delegation to discuss these issues. You must have known that?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: Yes. This I know because I received these invitations as a person responsible for protocol issues, but for your information I was involved mostly and primarily with technical issues, not with negotiations or political issues. And sometimes things developed so fast that I cannot always give you an answer. The fact is that I received these invitations and I signed that I received these invitations. I don't deny it I said. Eight years have passed since then. Whether he was the head of this group, I cannot ascertain.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And you must also know in that same context that this delegation had invited the Kosovar Albanian leaders and been refused at least 15 times. The Serbian delegation would come to Pristina and the Albanian delegation would not appear. You must know that?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: Yes, I recall that. And the question was about the venue of the meetings, because often we were asked to meet with them at a building of the Serbian government; and when I say we, I mean the Albanian delegation, refused to go to that place. It happened that they came to the office of Mr. Rugova; and once we went, Lord Owen and Mr. Vance from United States were responsible for the conference on the former Yugoslavia. This is, if I am not mistaken, how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Well, sir, I'm talking about 1998 and I don't believe that Vance and Owen were involved in this process at that time were they, in 1998?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: That's correct, but I brought this up because of the question of the venue for the meetings because that was a problem I didn't agree and I mentioned the occasion when we went there to that building. I also said that some meetings -- we refused some meetings because of the location and then we started to hold these meetings at the office of Mr. Rugova in Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Well, there was one meeting in Pristina with Dr. Rugova and the delegation headed by Professor Markovic and that was after the G5, the group that met with Mr. Milosevic in the spring of 1998, but that was the first and last time the Albanians leadership agreed and accepted an invitation to meet, to discuss a political solution in 1998. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: I cannot say yes because I don't remember what you are putting to me, neither the event nor the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And in answer to one of my questions, you said that the Albanian delegation refused to meet in the building of the Serbian government in Pristina, but the Albanian -- Kosovar Albanian leadership refused to meet anywhere. They wouldn't meet in Pristina. They wouldn't meet in Belgrade. They were invited to meet anywhere, any time, and they refused; correct?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: The Albanian side always insisted on the presence of the international factors at such meetings. As you might know, these meetings were proposed, but every time we were about to attend something happened. Something was not done that we required to be done, and that's why we have refused to attend.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, is this an appropriate time for the break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Merovci, we will have to interrupt the proceedings now for the day and resume tomorrow; that will be at 9.00. And as I indicated to you, we will ensure, even if it needs exceptional measures on our part and barring unforeseen events, we will ensure that we complete this cross-examination and any re-examination tomorrow. Overnight, it is very important that you have no discussion with anybody, anybody at all, about the evidence in the case. Obviously you're free to discuss any other matter with anybody you wish, but off-limits is any discussion of the evidence. So we will see you again tomorrow at 9.00. Meanwhile, could you leave the courtroom with the usher. Thank you. [The witness stands down].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: 9.00 tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 17th day of January, 2007, at 9.00 a.m.
